utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Matthias Neuner and Daryl Mundis assisted by our case manager Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the appearances for the Defence now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 4th of March, 2005, the 190th day of sitting, I bid good morning to all those present, the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence, the Accused, and all those present within and outside this courtroom. We will be hearing the testimony of a witness, but before we do that, would I like us to consider the plan for next week. So could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session, let me ask Madam Usher to bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Let me check that you are hearing the translation of my words in your own language. If so, tell me that you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called as a witness by the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic. Before asking you to read the solemn declaration, I need to know your name in order to avoid any errors that may occur. Can you give me your name, date and place of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Izet Mahir. I was born on the 5th of June, 1953 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a professional soldier, an officer in the army of the federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your rank and to which unit are you assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the rank of colonel, and I'm engaged in legal affairs of the command of the army of the federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, could you also tell us in 1992, 1993, what was your occupation at the time? Were you in the military? Where were you assigned, and was your rank.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're referring to the beginning of the war or before the war. I'm not sure I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell us what you were doing in 1992 and 1993. They are the two years that interest us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the beginning of the war, I was employed in the municipal legal department in Zenica. When the war started, I joined the Territorial Defence, that is on the 5th of December, 1992 [as interpreted]. And around the 8th of October, 1992, I joined the military police company of the district staff with changes that occurred in the BiH army. I worked in the military police battalion of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you testified in an international or national court of law about the events that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time for you to testify in a court law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today is the first time that I am appearing in court to testify about these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please read the solemn declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. Colonel, before giving the floor to the Defence attorneys, I need to give you some information about the procedure here. I think that some of the points I will refer to you are already familiar with because you worked in the legal services, so you have a minimum of knowledge at least about our procedure. Our procedure, which is inspired by the common law system is that first you will be asked to answer questions that will be put to you by the Defence attorneys, which you must have met in preparation for this hearing. Once those questions have been answered by you, once this examination-in-chief has been completed, the Prosecution seated to your right will have questions for you within what is known as the cross-examination, and the Prosecution will have at its disposal the same amount of time as the Defence for those questions, but you will be able to notice very quickly a difference in the nature of the questions. The Defence will put neutral questions to you, which will require commentaries which may be quite long from you. On the other hand, the Prosecution is allowed to put leading questions to you which may be answered by you with a yes or no. Once these questions from the Prosecution have been completed, the Defence will take the floor once again to ask you additional questions linked to the questions put to you by the Prosecution. The three Judges in front of you may, according to the Rules which have some continental law influence, too, can ask you questions at any point in time, but for the good procedure of the adversarial system we prefer you to answer the questions of both parties before we ask you any questions. It is quite possible we may not have any questions for you, because all the issues have been covered fully and you have provided clear answers. So there may be no need for any additional questions. But it is possible that we may ask you to clarify certain answers, or we may find that in the interest of justice you can fill in certain vacuums which require additional comment. I should like to remind you of two other points. You have taken the solemn declaration promising to tell the truth, the whole truth. You know what that means, so there's no need to insist on it, but I wish to highlight a specific feature of our procedure which is linked to the very status of the witness. If a witness believes that an answer to a question may later be used against him to incriminate him, the witness may say that he doesn't wish to answer that question. But under these very exceptional circumstances which we have never encountered, the Chamber may ask the witness to answer nonetheless, at the same time guaranteeing him immunity from prosecution. As you know, this is an oral procedure, which means that we have no written documents about what you are going to say except for a very brief summary as to why the Defence is calling you. Apart from that, we know nothing about you or about what you may say. Hence the importance of the answers that you will give. So please be as clear as possible. We know that as a general rule soldiers are very precise, so we don't expect any difficulty in that area. Should you fail to understand the meaning of a question, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it, because sometimes the questions may be complicated, and even the Judges may not fully understand the meaning of a question. So ask for it to be rephrased. Should you have any difficulty at all, don't hesitate to address us. Your testimony should be completed in the course of this morning, and I don't think it will go beyond that. But before giving the floor to the Defence, the Defence will tell us how much time they intend to use. I forgot to ask them this. So I give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence expects to complete its examination within an hour and 15 or an hour and a half, but I think it will be closer to one hour, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have no documents for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mahir. In addition to the cautions given to you by the president of the Trial Chamber, I need to remind you that we speak the same language, so of course you can answer my question as soon as I put it to you, but please wait a few seconds so that my question can be answered fully so that our friends in the courtroom and Their Honours can follow the proceedings easily. Before I pass on to questions, let me ask you a question that has already been asked by the president of the Trial Chamber, and I think on page 6, lines 5 to 6, an error has been committed. Could you tell us once again when you became a member of the Zenica Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: On the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The transcript recorded the 5th of December. That is why I wanted to correct that. You're working in the legal department, as you told the President of the Trial Chamber. What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I have a degree in law, and so I am an officer for normative and legal affairs in the joint command of the army of the federation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahir, did you serve in the JNA before the war, and did you have a rank in that army?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes. I did my regular military service in the JNA, and I got the rank of lance corporal, and afterwards I was in the reserve.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahir, since you said in answer to a question from the president of the Trial Chamber that you joined a military police battalion, were you involved in any policing before the war?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: No, I did not work in the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When in December 1992 you became a member of the military police battalion of the 3rd Corps after it was formed, tell me, what positions did you hold in the military police battalion?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: In the military police company, I was a military policeman. And at the very beginning when the battalion was formed, I was a military policeman. After that, I was an official engaged in investigations, and then I became a commander of a military police battalion, after that deputy commander of the military police battalion, and towards the end I was the acting commander of the military police battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, can you tell us who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: My immediate superior or the commander of the military police battalion was Mr. Zaim Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We apologise. We were just checking the transcript in English, and I think the translation is correct. In view of the fact that you were a member of the military police battalion of the 3rd Corps. For the needs of the Trial Chamber could you tell us what regulated the jurisdiction and tasks of the military police in those days.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: There were instructions for military police units, the Law on Criminal Procedure, the law on the work of military security, and instructions from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahir, could you now describe the tasks of the military police in that period of time, that is between 1991 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The tasks of the military police are regulated by the rules of service, and I shall try and be as clear as possible. They had to do with securing military -- senior military personnel and military facilities, then to control military traffic along roads, to secure important premises containing important documents and operations centres, then to prevent crime in the army, and then later to implement measures of military discipline, anti-sabotage protection, and the military police could be used, though we were not used, for fighting infiltrated sabotage groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Over whom was the military police in charge of when working to prevent criminal activity or detect the perpetrators of crimes?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The main duties as prescribed by rules and regulations is to work against the perpetrators of crimes but primarily military personnel. The military police could also act against civilians if military property was in jeopardy or if there were criminal offences for which the district military courts were responsible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please clarify that? It's clear that the military police could act vis-a-vis civilians if they jeopardise military property and facilities, but can you tell us what other crimes, as you say, would come under your jurisdiction, that is to say the military District Court, if crimes are perpetrated by civilians, what could the military police do in that respect? Could you give us examples of crimes of that kind?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: They are crimes which were listed in the bill that has the force of law with the military court. It's difficult for me to enumerate them all but I'll try. They are crimes against the state and system of a country, subversive acts, espionage acts against military facilities, and crimes against the armed forces. But as I say, a list of those exist. I'm sure you can come by that list because I don't think I can enumerate them now one by one here now. I might leave something out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a military policeman yourself and in connection with the military police and your tasks relating to discovering any criminal acts of members in the army, tell us in what situations did the -- was the military police active, could it go into action? What stage in that process faced with crimes perpetrated in that way?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The military police had a certain amount of autonomy in the pre-trial [Realtime transcript read in error "previous"] phase, and that is where the job of the military police came into play before a case was taken to trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This autonomy on the part of the military police, was it identical when this came to members of the army and when it came to civilians? Did it have the same autonomy and jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The military police had complete authority over military personnel. However, and perhaps I forgot to say this a moment ago, the military police when it had December with the military police it had to ask assistance from the Ministry of Internal Affairs. It itself did not have the authority to interrogate civilians or work with civilians in that way. It had to ask the help of the organs in the interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of this authority, that is to say to work autonomously in the pre-trial stage --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there seems to be an error in the interpretation here so let me ask the witness another question to clarify that point, because in line 12 -- on page 12, line 23, some words appear which the witness did not utter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So I should like to ask Mr. Mahir you something else now. Let me ask you again. Did the military police have the same degree of autonomy working in the pre-trial stage with members of the army, army personnel, and when it had dealings with the civilians which had perpetrated acts which come under the authority of the District Court.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I said that the military police was completely autonomous when it came to members of the military but when we were dealing with crimes perpetrated by civilians then this would be crimes provided for by war. It -- by law. It asked for the assistance and worked in cooperation with the organs of the internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. It seems that there are some mistakes that have been cropping up here. In line -- on page 12, line 17, it says "in the previous trial phrase."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter said pre-trial phase and we're talking -- says the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking about the pre-trial phase, before a criminal file is brought. That is "pre-trial" not "previous trial." I think that has been corrected and I do apologise, but we have to be certain of the details that crop up in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Mahir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see in the English according to the French translation they said we were autonomous. I don't know. In your language what word was used. Could he tell us what he means, autonomous with respect to what? To the civilian authorities, or with respect to his own hierarchy, because there is an ambiguity there. Perhaps we need clarification on that point. What is meant by the word autonomy, because the translation of the word can allow us to suppose any number of things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have heard, Mr. Mahir, what the president of the Trial Chamber has just asked you. When you spoke about autonomy in your acts with respect to military personnel, what do you mean by that? In what way were you autonomous?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Well, the rules of service for military security and the works of the military police were prescribed -- prescribed the competencies of the military police. When I say autonomous I mean we didn't have to ask agreement by the civilian organs in doing our work. If we did our work according to the rules of service and instructions. Then we would apply authorisations given to us provided to us by the war -- by the law. I'm sorry. We didn't have to ask for anybody's agreement on -- from the civilian authorities. So when I say autonomous, in keeping with the law governing the work of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And if we wanted to show this by highlighting an example, if you wish to give us an example, for example, if somebody said something is being stolen from a house, for example, and that it is assumed that a military member of the staff was doing this, then what autonomous actions could you undertake?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: In we had a report of that kind as the investigation -- we had a duty service that functioned round the clock 24 hours. If a call came in that way, we wouldn't have to ask anybody's agreement and accord to send in an intervention unit and to send in the authorised military personnel to go on the spot to determine what was going on and to prevent a crime and if necessary to take the perpetrator into custody if they had committed acts against the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you also said that when crimes were perpetrated for which civilians were responsible and taken to the District Court that you then worked together with the civilian police. So I should now like you to tell us in view of the examples that you have just quoted this: If for example you were to learn that a civilian had broken into a military equipment warehouse, for example, belonging to one of your units, for instance, what would you do? How would you act in that particular case?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: If circumstances allowed and in this case they certainly wouldn't allow for that in the example you quoted, we would intervene straight away. We would try and prevent what was going on and take the individual into custody and prevent a crime from being committed. We would call up the unit and the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the operative work would be alongside their presence with people from the internal affairs. So we would act straight away and not wait for them to arrive.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But at any rate, if there was any doubt that a civilian had engaged in some crime which came under the competencies of the military court as you have explained you would either do so immediately or when the conditions were ripe. You would continue to work alongside with the civilian police force; is that right? You would cooperate with them?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, 100 per cent, precisely as you have just put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now, please, Mr. Mahir, if one was to learn or there was any doubt or suspicions that a crime had been committed and that the investigating judge would go on the spot on site, could you tell us what the situation would be with respect to the members of the military police?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: If a situation of that kind occurred, and they did occur, the military police, once an investigating duty judge would go out onto the spot, the military police would work exclusively upon the orders of the duty investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In situations in which some material, for example, which could indicate the existence of a crime being perpetrated and pinpoint a perpetrator, if this comes into the hands of the prosecutor, what would then be the role and position of the military police, for instance?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Well, according to our law, the law prescribes in fact that the pre-trial investigation should be conducted by the prosecutor. So if a criminal report were to reach the prosecutor or knowledge reach him that something was done which would constitute a crime, the military police would then work according to the instruction and requests of the prosecutor. So it would be the prosecutor who would be in charge of the pre-trial process.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahir, if somebody had committed a crime and a criminal -- criminal action was taken for an investigation to be conducted into that crime, what role in that particular case and in what way would the military police act?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: In that stage, that is to say the military police would work pursuant to the instructions of the investigating judge, because it is not up to us to collect information. We do so pursuant to orders and instructions from the investigating judge in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Those were some general questions and I should like now to go back to the battalion of the military police of the 3rd Corps. Tell me this, please, Mr. Mahir, how was the battalion organised, the battalion of the military police, in 1993? How was that organised?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The battalion of the military police along with certain amendments but always had four companies. In a subsequent phase it was expanded but you're talking about 1993, so there were three companies, a unit for anti-terrorist activities and a platoon for investigations. So that would be the composition of the battalion itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, briefly explain to us what the scope of work of the companies was and what the other units of the battalion of the military police that you have just mentioned did.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that the tasks of the military police and the scope of their work was regulated by the services of the military police, and I'll try and say that the first company did patrol work and escort work escorting individuals. The second company worked for the -- providing security details of facilities and individuals. The third company was engaged -- well, that unit in fact most often was used in 1993 in the zone of combat operations, but if they were in town they would be used for patrol servicing and also as a security service as well. The fourth company was the traffic company in fact which was in charge of traffic security or controlled traffic on the roads and the Anti-Terrorist Unit in the first stage was just an expanded -- was a small department but was trained in the course of 1993 and strengthened, but it was a unit which built up its image in disciplining the army. That is to say ensuring patrol work, the patrol services, effecting control over military discipline and sometimes providing security for high-ranking military officials. And then the military political investigations platoon, that was perhaps the professional part, the sole section that did police work. Translated into police -- into everyday terms it did policing and police work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that from the very beginning you yourself were a member of the battalion of the military police of the 3rd Corps, could you tell us what the cadres were like? How many members did the battalion have in 1993? What personnel? What members did it have?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The military police in fact or the battalion of the military police was established on the basis of the district staff and the platoon there, and it was from the Municipal Staff that had been disbanded. It received members from there, and they were brought to the battalion as were other people from the combat unit. So at the beginning it numbered about 230 to 250 people. That was the maximum number. But as the tasks increased and the requirements grew, we had a full complement which was about 450 to 480 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said that the most professional part, if I can put it that way or I think you put it that way, the part we would be interested in in the criminal proceedings section, was the part of the battalion which dealt with police investigations. Tell me -- us, please, how many members were there -- were engaged in police investigations, military police investigations, and what was their job? What was their task?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Police investigations numbered about 20 to 22 or 3 men, and I said that within the military police investigations, we had the duty service which was operational, which had six soldiers, six soldiers providing round the clock 24 hour duty service much then we had authorised people in the military police, 8 to 10 soldiers there, eight to ten members. We also had lawyers who tried to organise and coordinate the work and compile criminal reports and dealt with the legal aspects of this job, and there were between four to six of these men. Then we had the crime technicians, two men there, two crime technicians. And that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Mahir, please, the people in the military police, whether we're dealing with members of the companies or the particular services to prevent crime and detect crime, before they would take up their duties there did they have any professional experience or knowledge in military police work? Were they trained in that way?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: A limiting factor was the replenishment of cadres. The BH army was created and established as it was under the conditions that prevailed, and the same thing was reflected on the police. There were very few people in the military police that had been specially trained as military policemen and educated as military policemen. A very small number. Two or three people had just come to us from the MUP, for instance, joined the military police having worked in the MUP previously, and usually they were retired people who had expressed a desire to move to the military police and work there. Or for whatever reason. Some people from Orasje for example left the police there for reasons that were known and then came to Zenica. They didn't find jobs there and then they became members of the military police. But I think that this cadre profile expressed in percentages would be very small. Of a total number, 10 per cent at the most had any knowledge beforehand in police work or were trained and educated in police work. So that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To what extent was the corps command aware of the situation and did it make efforts to see that people were trained to work in the battalions, people work in the battalions receive additional training to bring them up to scratch if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Well, this sound quite improbable but as soon as the units were formed and when the fighting was going around Zenica and all over Bosnia-Herzegovina in fact, the corps command issued a number of orders by which they should become organised. Military policemen should undergo police training and also specialised training, and at a certain stage during 1993, agreement was asked from the MUP and assist -- the MUP offered assistance for training crime technicians. We just had one camera, for example, and that was the entire state of the equipment we had for crime technicians. So -- and later on, people were brought in who did have some professional military knowledge. One man was a military prosecutor, for example, in the JNA, and he was a member of the police later on and joined the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Mahir, let us see how the chain of command functioned. What was the chain of command with respect to the military police battalion? Who were the superior officers in relation to you as members and in relation to the battalion as an entity of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The commander of the battalion was its commander. I said a moment ago Mr. Zaim Mujezinovic was the commander of the battalion. It was a staff unit of the 3rd Corps, and the commander was in command of the brigades and all the other units, and he was also in command of the battalion of the military police through its specialised body the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So the commander commands through the security organ. Tell me, can the commander sometimes make a decision regarding the engagement of the military police?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The commander may make all decisions independently. If he did, it may have been to militarily engage the battalion of the military police. But if a military police battalion company was to be sent somewhere, it had to go through the chief of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the corps commander commanded the military police via the security organ. Tell me, how did the chief of the military police security organ or the commander of the 3rd Corps, how did he command units through the security organ?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The rules of service prescribed from the very beginning that the senior commander is the specialised body through which the commander exercises his function, and the chief of security, because that is what he actually was, was the most responsible person for combat readiness of military police units. And military security service chose personnel, their training, their resources, and means. Those were one of the ways for military police units to carry out the task -- their tasks through instructions from the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, Mr. Mahir, the President of the Trial Chamber using the example of the autonomy that you used referred to your tasks in the pre-trial procedure. Tell us what were the tasks of the military police in the pre-trial procedures? Could you describe that for us, please? What did you actually do?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the military police had the same tasks as organs of internal affairs. I shall try and be as clear as possible. Having learnt that there is grounds to suspect that a criminal offence had been committed, it was the duty of the military police, that is their investigators, to find the perpetrator of the criminal offence, to find clues and traces, to protect them, and then later in the criminal procedure phase he would act in accordance with the instructions of the judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You just said, Mr. Mahir, that it was your duty to collect information. Tell me, could you interview certain people or interrogate them as witnesses or was your role different according to the law?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The military police does not have the right to interrogate persons. It collects information that will help in dealing with the case. And had any statements been taken, they couldn't be used in trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What happened with statements that you took from persons if a criminal procedure was instituted?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I said that as such they couldn't be used in criminal proceedings, but they could be used by the prosecutor to ask for additional information and to channel the work of the military police, to provide guidelines to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Once you had clues that a certain person may have committed an offence, what measures would you take for that person to be taken to justice?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Perpetrators are different. Criminal offences are different. If we were to find out that a person had made an offence, we would try and identify him and take him into custody. When that was not possible, we'd issue a wanted poster in the aim of bringing that person to justice either for disciplinary sanctions or criminal sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How did you forward the information you collected to other bodies that were responsible for processing these cases?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Through regular exchanges of reports, exchanges of information, through -- we would address regular reports to the military security organ daily, weekly, and monthly, and even annually. Then if it had to do with criminal reports, these would be filed with the courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Mahir, did the military police battalion -- was it the only military police within the 3rd Corps or were there some military police units in other military units as well?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Military police battalion was the battalion of the 3rd Corps, but every entity of the level of a brigade had a military police unit. The mountain brigades had platoons, the motorised brigade had companies of military police, then there were provisional formations of operations groups, which as a rule did not have military police units, but because they were far from Zenica, the operations group of Bosanska Krajina was allowed to form a military police company.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the military police battalion of the 3rd Corps have superiority over these companies or platoons in lower-level units?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: No. The military police battalion had no superior function because these units were commanded by the commanders of the units. Of course, through their specialised security organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Even though you were not superior to these military units in the brigades, which were commanded by their commanders through their security organs, did you have any relations with those units? Did you have any kind of jurisdiction towards them?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: In a later stage of the formation of the military police battalion following orders of the command of the 3rd Corps and in line with the plans made by the military security service, the military police battalion engaged in training of these smaller units and also in providing equipment. A certain part of the equipment for the battalion would be given to these units. And also if instructions were given by the chief of military security or the corps commander, we could be sent and were sent to the areas of responsibility of certain brigades when we provided assistance, professional assistance, in carrying out police work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If in a particular area a certain criminal offence were to be committed, what were the competencies of the military police unit of the brigade stationed in that area?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: If that happened in their area of responsibility, they were the competent unit. In that case, that unit would act. If it didn't have the capacity, and quite frequently this did happen, they could address themselves for assistance, and then in -- the chief of the security service might send their officers to assist them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to a previous question from me, Mr. Mahir, you told us when the military police could act in relation to civilians. Tell me, who would normally protect public law and order, lawfulness, protection of civilians in the whole area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps? Whose competence was that? Or to be more precise, was the military police responsible for the overall security situation in the area of 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: It was not responsible for the overall security situation. The civilian police would implement the curfew, and we would assist them, too, sometimes in patrols. But on the free territory in-depth the military police of the 3rd Corps was not responsible for overall security. But if we're talking about military police work, military police work in the town of Zenica itself, the military police was in a sense following orders of the corps commander responsible for the activities of other services, crime prevention, patrolling the town, implementing military discipline measures. For that, the military police of the 3rd Corps in Zenica itself was responsible for security in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In those situations implementing the 3rd Corps order, tell me what kind of cooperation you had with the security services centre and the police station in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I can say that our relations were correct. They had their terms of reference. We had ours. So we cooperated well with the MUP. We had to cooperate with them because we relied frequently on the MUP because our equipment was practically non-existent. So their assistance was indispensable.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you spoke about the number of members of the military police battalion. Tell me, what was the ethnic composition of that battalion and to what extent the 3rd Corps Commander insisted on maintaining such an ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: This may be my personal judgement, but I believe that military police battalion was one of the few units that -- in which all ethnicities were represented from the beginning until the end. I know that there were people of Orthodox and Catholic faith. Therefore, all the ethnic groups were represented. To what extent the commander had an influence over this, well, if the commander felt that its composition was not appropriate, it could have asked for changes. I do know that from the beginning until the end, it was mixed and, in fact, the number of Croats and Serbs increased in 1994 in relation to 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were speaking about certain competencies of the military police battalion in town, tell me to what extent you cooperated with military police platoons of brigades stationed in town and whether crime prevention by the military was exclusively the task of the battalion or was it also done in cooperation with military police platoons of brigades.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: If you're referring to the city of Zenica itself, I said that the command of the 3rd Corps issued an order with the aim of preventing any unlawful actions. For example, false identity or taking insignia of the military police of the 3rd Corps. And for that reason, the commander ordered that military police platoons should deal with only three matters, and that is to provide security of the facilities and persons in their unit, to patrol their own areas of activity, to do reception work, but not to patrol the city or to implement any other measures. But if we had soldiers, deserters from the 303rd Brigade, for instance, then they would have to deal with it, because we had too much to do anyway as compared to the units of the 1st and 2nd Corps and also the 303rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Mahir, in 1993, did the military police at any point in time have superiority over the civilian police and take over its competencies, or were relationships between them relationships of cooperation throughout?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The military police never had any superior position in relation to other bodies, especially not over the civilian police. How could it when they were much larger than we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were working on detection and prevention of crime, tell me, Mr. Mahir, what was the policy of the 3rd Corps and its commander with respect to measures to prevent crime and especially with regard to measures to detect and prosecute the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I hope I have made a sufficient pause this time. Yes, thank you. I was a bit confused. I forgot your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Since you were working in a part of the battalion dealing with crime prevention, what was the policy and to what extent that was the position of the 3rd Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: In addition to what was prescribed by law, we were one of the rare services that had heightened measures, stricter measures. Every effort was made to prevent crime. But should crime be committed, it was almost impossible to seek out the perpetrators. I don't know whether it's appropriate for me to say that members of the military police from Zenica to Visoko would hitchhike. There were very few motor vehicles on the road. So to go to Visoko to collect information was a problem for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In conducting your stringent measures and requests from your commander to do everything to prevent the perpetration of crimes and uncover the perpetrators, what problems did you encounter? You gave us one example. You said you didn't have any vehicles, and you had to do the journey as you described. What other problems did you encounter in that -- that year of 1993 which made it difficult for you to comply with the stringent instructions given to you?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: We had numerous problems. Some were objective, some were not, but most of them -- when I say subjective problems, those were problems that were conditioned by the wartime circumstances that we couldn't influence. But the constant displacements of the population, migration -- population migrations, a large number of people in Zenica. At one point it had over 120.000 there. More than 60, 70 per cent of the people had come in from different areas. Most of them had no documents, no proof of identity of any kind. Many people wore uniforms. Some people would come by in military uniforms. Some of them didn't wish to take to off even when they went to sleep. So you had situations of that kind. And we were amassing a data under areas controlled by the HVO in 1992, 1993, 1994 and even 1995, for example. Then there was fighting going on, combat operations, lack of ammunition and weapons and everything else, which made the situation very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With respect to the strict orders that were given to you, and I repeat that, orders that you must carry out your tasks and duties, were there any exceptions in the policies of the 3rd Corps Command and its commander, for example? Was there an order according to which you should not implement military/political measures of investigation? Were any people except from that?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: No. Not a single member of the army was except from these rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me now, please, Mr. Mahir, in 1993 how were the members of the army held responsible and for what offences?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Well, some -- this might seem a bit strange as misdemeanours, but they were sanctioned, disciplines was in force. They were discipline. That's what we did in the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And who decided whether we were dealing with petty offences, misdemeanors or whatever?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The military courts did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who decided on the disciplinary measures to be enforced and sanctions and sentences?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: This kind of discipline was conducted according to the rules of service governing discipline, and this was decided on by the superior officers and the military courts. So members of the army would be held responsible for crimes, depending on their gravity, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For a discipline offence, what kind of sentences could be meted out?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I have already said the rules set this out. The commander of platoon, battalion, command, and so on could issue measures of this kind. They would either be reprimanded, issued reprimands, given duty work to do, and more stringent measures, too. So it was the commander who would issue a stay in prison of up to 30 days, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what about disciplinary offences?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The commander would be in charge there for more serious forms, and he could mete out prison sentences of up to 60 days, but usually it was the disciplinary courts that issued sentences of that kind in cases of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There seems to have been a mistake somewhere but I can't find it so I'll deal with it later on. How else could these soldiers be held responsible and in fact how did they -- how were they held accountable in 1993 for any offences?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: In addition to this kind of offence, the petty offences, misdemeanours and so on there was criminal responsibility as well for more serious crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the organ there who was in charge and who would deal with more serious cases, that is to say with crimes?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: For Zenica it would be the military District Court in Zenica. So military District Courts were set up and it was their responsibility to deal with more serious cases committed by members of the military. If they were co-perpetrators, if there was a military person co-perpetrating a crime with a civilian, then this would be handed over to the civilian courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but on page 31, line 3 there is a word omitted or words omitted, criminal responsibility. So there were different types of responsibility and criminal responsibility were the words missing there. So I'd just like to make a note of that and have that corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how often, to the best of your recollections did the members of the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the 3rd Corps in 1993 were disciplined and held accountable and punished? How many people, members of the army were punished in 1993 for any offences?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: In 1993, I think hundreds of them but I'm just giving you out that kind of figure. But I didn't expect the question. But you could look that up and see how many people had custodial sentences. But in 1993, several hundred.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you yourself were a policeman, soldier, tell me, please, the members of the military police, were they privileged in any way or exempt from any disciplinary measures or from being punished for acts -- acting contrary to the law or contrary to orders?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, not only were we privileged but our members were sanctioned more stringently than the members of other units and we wouldn't comment on that amongst themselves. And say that in addition to all the difficulties a military policeman faced in going about his duties, in addition to all that, if he were to do something that was contrary to discipline and the Criminal Code they would be held accountable far more stringently than anybody else and I could give you countless examples, very characteristic examples. For example, for an offence in another unit you might not have been punished at all. You might have just been reprimanded, whereas a member of the military police would be re-commanded to another combat unit as far away as possible from his place of residence in most cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In going about your duties as a military policeman, you have already told us the problems you encountered in your job, but tell me now, please, to what extent did these problems affect your ability to detect crimes and the period of time necessary to elucidate certain acts that had been committed?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I've already said that this depended on the type of crime or misdemeanour or offence that was committed, the type of act. There were acts that you could unravel in the space of several hours, whereas for others you needed operative work with cooperation among crime -- with Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. crime technicians, and then this would go on for seven or eight months sometimes, as long as that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you quote some examples in which the battalion of the military police was engaged, involved, over a period of several months in order to uncover and prevent the criminal acts of certain groups, for example?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes, I can quote you a case in point of a complete unit. The Green Legion, the 314th Brigade, a unit which almost the whole it have was under the commander, the deputy commander of the staff. It was a crime group and behave -- they behaved as criminals at that particular stage, but we had to find proof. We had to prove it. And some of the knowledge that we gathered were linked to April 1993, but to take these individuals to justice and to take them into custody, we didn't succeed in doing until January 1994. For example, there was another characteristic case, a member of the 7th Muslim unit which was called, I thought, the mountain guerrilla or the Sokol group, unit, falcon group, and a group that engaged in crime sometime towards the end of May, for example. And we were able only in September and October to collect the data necessary to show us who the perpetrators were, and I think it was only in 1994 that they were brought to justice. But they were taken into custody towards the end of 1993. So that was another case in point. This guerrilla, the Turkish guerrilla, counter-intelligence work, security services and the military police battalion was just used as a unit to realise the final stages of that settling of accounts. I don't know if I was clear enough in explaining that. If not, I shall be happy to explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I have understood you correctly, you said that that you received information that certain individuals were engaging in crime on a continuous basis, and then you did all the work necessary to bring them to justice and after many months you were able to collect sufficient evidence and proof in order to bring a lawsuit against them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You gave us three examples. One example was the members of the 7th and then the Green Legion belonging to the 314th and as a result of work with the counter-intelligence service and military security of the 3rd Corps. That was the Turkish guerrilla that you mentioned. Now, tell me, these individuals, these perpetrators, were criminal reports filed later on and were criminal proceedings undertaken against them all?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes, against all of them. These were the most characteristic cases, and everybody was held accountable. Some were brought before the district military courts, others between the regular civilian courts, but they were all brought to justice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you mentioned the Turkish guerrilla and said it was the result of operational work of the counter-intelligence service, tell me, please, whether those foreigners, in view of the acts that they were held accountable for, were they within any units, within the composition of any units or were they independent units before -- because as far as I can see the first groups came under the brigade, the composition of the brigade of the 1st -- 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: As to the Turkish guerrilla, I was never quite -- I never quite knew about its status. People joined up with them, people who found some refuge there or protection in that unit. I don't really know. But as it was counter intelligence, the counter-intelligence department, I don't really know what their actual status was but we did take part together with them in bringing people to justice. So therefore I might assume that they were members of -- well, I don't really know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, from the beginning of the work of the military police, when it started working, what attitude did the 3rd Corps have towards cooperating with the Croatian Defence Council, for example, and towards protecting some property -- property belonging to the Croatian people, religious property and other religious and cultural monuments?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Well, at the -- at the very beginning when the military police battalion was established we were told that our district staff company would be the basic point and the HVO corresponding units. Now, why we didn't do that, why we didn't set up a joint unit, I don't know. It -- this cooperation never came about. Now, as regards mutual relationships, many of our members in different stages had some very -- if I can put it, say, ugly pressure from members of the -- of -- from Croatian -- from the Croatian ethnicity. A man called Mario who was a deputy commander of the military police, for example, for the first few months in 1993 and then after what happened to Mr. Breko [phoen] in Busovaca and Sasa Stjepanovic, the man left the army. He left. He joined some humanitarian organisation and no longer was a member of the army. Now, as protection, you mentioned something about the protection of -- of monuments. There were orders according to which certain facilities from the Catholic and Orthodox churches. Both the civilian police and the military police guarded Orthodox churches or Catholic churches and the monastery at Guca Gora, for example, is a case in point.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I ask you about the Guca Gora case, let's just make things clearer. You said that Croatian members in the battalion, there was certain pressures being -- there was certain pressure being exerted against these Croatian members. Now, the members of the Bosniak people did you expert pressure on them or was there some other pressure exerted on these Croatian members that you wanted to explain?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Unfortunately I'm sorry for that because the Judge said at the beginning that as a soldier, he expect immediate to be clear. No, it was the HVO members that exerted pressure on our members, the members of the battalion of the military police. Croat members who were in our battalion. It was the HVO exerting pressure on them. So I apologise for not being clear enough. Zoran, for example, or some other members. I never had myself any qualms or queries at all. We were all --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, anyway, Mr. President, I think that this would be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 10.30. We're going to take the technical break now in order to allow the witness and the technical staff to take a break or do the necessary -- make the necessary technical adjustments in the meantime, and we'll reconvene at five to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. The give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahir, in answer to my previous questions, you said that in certain situations, you were engaged for special assignments. Tell me, if my understanding is correct, you started out as an ordinary military policeman; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any tasks as a military policeman at the end of January 1993 in connection with certain combat operations that were happening in the village of Dusina?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes, I did have the assignment that as a member of the 1st company of the military police battalion to go there with the company commander to escort certain people from the area of combat operations to the KP Dom in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who those persons were?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: They were members of the HVO captured in combat in the surroundings of Dusina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How did you transport those captured members of the HVO, and where did you take them from to the KP Dom in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: As members of the 1st company, we went to Lasva. A group went to the school in Lasva and took over custody. I wasn't at the school. I was near the bus, the vehicle. So I didn't go to the school. They picked them up and drove them to the bus. We boarded them on the bus and drove to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were transporting those captured members of the HVO from Lasva to Zenica, did any of the military policemen who were with you or you personally, did you mistreat those HVO members?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did any member of the HVO whom you were transporting by bus complain to you because of harassment?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I must admit that we didn't converse with them, but no one complained to us. We were travelling by bus, 10 or 15 people boarded the bus, there wasn't much talk, and we transported them to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a military policeman, did any of the captured HVO soldiers say to you or one of your colleagues that any persons had been killed? Did they give you any intimations of that?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: No one said anything to that effect to me. After we had transported those prisoners to the KP Dom and handed them over, I didn't meet them again, but I do know that the next day our members during investigations did have interviews with them, but I don't know that anyone said anything about any murders. There were dead on both sides in combat. We knew that even before we left for Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the investigating judge or the prosecutor ever ask you as members of the military police to carry out any kind of additional inquiries in connection with the events in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Me personally, no. But I do know that two or three days after the combat operations, I think a commission was formed. I think somebody from the department of military police investigations went to Dusina, and I think the next day the Civil Defence carried out assignation of the battlefield. That's as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sanitation of the battlefield. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. This is something that is not clear here. You said that the Civil Defence carried out sanitation of the battlefield, cleared the battlefield. That is on page 39, line 6. Who was legally responsible for sanitisation of the areas?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The Civil Defence, wherever that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are probably familiar with the broader area of Lasva, Dusina, and the surrounding villages. Tell me, did anyone from the Civil Defence inform you, the military police, that when bodies were found in that whole area there were any suspicions that they may have died in some other way and not in combat?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I am not aware of any of our members having gained any such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahir, do you have any knowledge at all about what happened after the kidnapping of Zivko Totic in April 1993 in Zenica and whether the military police had any kind of assignments in that connection and, if so, which?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I do know that Mr. Zivko Totic was kidnapped in Podbrezje. There's a monument there to the escorts who were escorting him. I must say that this was shocking piece of news that somebody was kidnapped and especially that the escort was killed. The military police first, as well as HVO policemen, went on-site investigation, and then they had a slightly broader assignment that each one of us should, through our daily activities, and some were members of commissions who went to tour the area, we were all asked to collect information linked to that event.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahir, do you know whether the military police carried out these orders and tried to collect information? Are you aware of the kind of information that was obtained?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: As I said, the military police accompanied these joint commissions formed by the corps command that toured the villages around Zenica expecting to find them there. I think the whole battalion was allotted to this task. This went on for four or five days. And then we were tasked to stop the search four or five days later because allegedly, I don't know whether in fact, that the kidnappers had got in touch with the European Monitors and that the monitors had asked the search to be stopped in the interest of the safety of the person kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did the military police battalion or any other segment of the military forces of the 3rd Corps involved in the kidnapping of Zivko Totic?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, I can't say no a hundred per cent for any other entity, but as far as the military police battalion is concerned, I can claim with certainty that no one had anything to do with the kidnapping except for the processes that took place afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If Zivko Totic testifying in this court were to say that a special unit of the 3rd Corps or, rather, of the security of the 3rd Corps took part in his kidnapping, tell me first, was there any such special unit, and secondly, do you know anything at all about that?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I would be pleased if the 3rd Corps had marines or commandos or these special units. We didn't have a proper police unit, never mind special police. No such unit ever existed. There were no special units. In the 3rd Corps, as far as I know, there was no unit that would -- could be described as a special unit, because I'm familiar with the criteria they would have to fulfil. So no such unit existed in the 3rd Corps, and particularly not in the military police battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you reject any possibility of a police unit of the 3rd Corps ever thinking about a kidnapping, never mind carrying it out. Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes. I think I was quite clear as the President of the Chamber asked me to be. No unit of the military police took part in that kidnapping or any other.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you mentioned Guca Gora. Tell me, please, did you and upon whose orders take part in providing security for the monastery at Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I personally was involved. I was tasked by my commander, and I assume the task came from the 3rd Corps Command that together with 16 men that we go in a minibus to the Guca Gora area to secure the monastery at Guca Gora. Upon arriving there near the command of the 306th Brigade, I saw there was a command post there. I assume it was of the 306th Brigade. Another squad of the 306th Brigade joined us, and with some difficulty we managed to enter the facility and to secure the facility for and month and a month and a half, until August. I was there for only a couple of days though.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you left, who was threatening that facility so that you had to engage the Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: On site we came across several foreigners, Arabs. They didn't speak our language. They spoke Arabic, which I don't understand. But in any event, they were not locals. There were a couple of local people, maybe 15 or 20 among those we saw, and at the very entrance there was a kind of machine-gun nest, a person manning it, and a position fortified. So this was a group of people who were within the monastery of Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Upon your request, did they leave immediately or did you have some difficulty in taking over control of the facility?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: This reached a point -- I don't know whether incident is the proper word, but it was really very tense. We were about to fire because we were tasked to enter and secure the Guca Gora monastery because these persons allegedly wanted to blow it up. So we had to carry out that task. There was no choice. I had to do it. After a couple of hours and some squabbling and threatening and posing of conditions, we managed to enter the monastery.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice whether there was any damage to the monastery?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: There was damage to the monastery. There were books thrown around. There were some objects in front of the monastery. In one of the halls, I think a piece of the organ was broken off. There was some inscriptions in Arabic, wine spilt and things like that. That is what we could see at first glance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did members of the army try to put in order the mess made by the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: About early evening, a gentleman came. I don't know him personally, but I know his name. Mr. Beba came. I think he was in the operations group or in Travnik. I don't know what his status was. He came with a group of people to paint over the graffiti, and we assisted, though I left the next day in the evening. So I don't know personally what happened later on. I just know that in August our unit came to Zenica and that this squad of the 306th remained securing the monastery and then handed it over to the church authorities when the conditions were ripe for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That ends my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have the other Defence team any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at this point in time we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Mr. President, in view of the fact that the witness mentioned an order - I didn't expect him to say that - I have that order in the B/C/S. May I be allowed to show him this order, and if the witness recognises it, I would be glad to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I didn't provide the document to the Prosecution nor anybody else because I didn't think that witness would know anything about the document. Perhaps the witness could read through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I understand the situation, there's an order of some kind, I don't know who from, which you have in your possession, and the witness mentioned an order in the course of his testimony. Now you would like to show the witness this order for him to say whether he recognises it or not. So that's the situation. Mr. Mundis, you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps if we could have a look at the order. I don't know the date of the order. The witness has mentioned several orders. I have no idea even a rough time period.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me explain. The witness said during the evidence that at one point General Hadzihasanovic had issued an order according to which a military police battalion would take over certain authorisation of the platoons of military police in the town of Zenica. And during the break I managed to look through my documents, and I'd just like to see if the witness can state whether that was the order he had in mind when he said what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We would have no objection to the document being shown to the witness. I would ask, though, in the future if my learned colleague discovers documents during the breaks if perhaps we could get a little more advanced notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we also have a look at the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're going to show it to Mr. Dixon as well. I assume that the order is in B/C/S; right? Perhaps we could place it on the ELMO, and the witness could read it, and that will facilitate matters for one and all. Very well. No objections from you, Mr. Dixon? No, none?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that was precisely what I was going to suggest. It's not a long order. Perhaps he could read it out. We're going to hear it, and the witness will be able to say whether it was indeed the order that he referred to, whether it is indeed the order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the order I was referring to. It is the order by which the authorisations were restricted of the platoons of the military police, and I'd like to read it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Because of instances of abuse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead. Read it. Read it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Due to the abuse of the official position -- of official positions on the part of members of the units of military police located in the area of Zenica, it is necessary for us to warn you about the use and deployment of military police units in the spirit of the rules and regulations governing the work of the military police in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In view of the fact in the area of the town of Zenica there is a battalion of the military police existent there and linked to the need for the members of the units of the military police in your unit I order the following." And point one is: "The units of the military police belonging to your units may be deployed exclusively for tasks stipulated in chapter 1, paragraph 2.6, and they are as follows: "One, the organisation of shift duty patrols and reconnoitering points, and physical security for command posts. "Second, within the frameworks of the commands, the operative centre and the communications centre and the encryption centre should be established for documents, organisation of control points for controlling exits and entrances to the command post can search the area and premises which the commands are required to take over and to ensure that these have been properly examined. "2. All other tasks from the area of work of the military police come under the competency of the battalion of the military police. "3. The assistant commander for security in the unit shall be held responsible for the proper handling of the military police units." And then it says in the signature, "The commander Enver Hadzihasanovic."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the date? Can you see the date when the order was issued?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The 23rd of October, 1993, is the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the witness has recognised this document, may it be marked for identification until we receive a translation in English of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The signature there, is it the signature of the commander of the 3rd Corps or is it somebody who signed for him, for the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not quite sure whether this is the commander's signature. I would -- I think it's signed for the commander. I don't think it's the commander's happened writing and signature. I think somebody signed for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As it's a document having to do with the military police, the -- in the contents, the intellectual contents of the order, was it compiled in the military police battalion or not? And we see the IM/TA. What is that IM/TA? What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: IM/TA are the initials of the person that put the document together. It was not done in the military police battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You want a number, an identification number, do you, Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What about the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, may we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be DH2052, and the date is the 23rd of October, 1993. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the other Defence counsel? Would they like to ask any questions with respect to the document, because there was the 7th Muslim Brigade stamp on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We said earlier on that we had no questions, but since the document has appeared in the meantime, I would like to show the document to the witness once again. He didn't read it out fully.
