utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mahir, would you take a look at the upper right-hand corner, who the addressee is, who this was accept to.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: It was sent to the organ of security, the security organ of the 7th Muslim Brigade. If you mean the stamp in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the upper right hand document. It is a 3rd Corps document. Who was if addressed to? Only to the 7th Muslim Brigade or other units, too?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: No, to all units in the area of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Not just to the 7th Muslim Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: And that's what it says, to the command of the units located and stationed in Zenica. I forgot to say that. That's this part here, the right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm now going to give the floor to the Prosecution for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would ask, Madam Usher, if you could perhaps leave that there. I'm going to ask the witness some questions about that in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Daryl Mundis. My name is Daryl Mundis, and along with my colleagues here we represent the Prosecution this morning. I'm going to ask you a number of questions. Before I do so, however, I would ask if you don't understand any of my questions, simply tell me that and I'll rephrase them. It's not my intention in any way to confuse you with any of the questions that I'm going to ask you about today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would also ask if Madam Usher could move the ELMO or at least move it back a bit perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me start, sir, with this document that is before you now since it's still here. Can you tell us, sir, in 1993, up to the time period this document was written, that is in October 1993, other than the 3rd Corps military police battalion, what other military police units of any other brigades of the 3rd Corps were present in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I said that a moment ago in addition to the military police battalion and the brigade in its organic composition, there were units of the military police. And in addition to the battalion of the military police of the 3rd Corps, there was also a unit of the military police of the 7th Muslim Brigade and a unit of the military police of the 303rd Brigade, and another of the 314th Brigade, a company of the 301st Brigade as well, a unit of that, because that was in existence still at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's talk about each of these different brigades and their military police companies individually. How many military policemen of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade were, if you will, stationed in Zenica? How many of them were there and where were they?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: To my knowledge, about one platoon of the military police. That needn't be exact. I didn't have an insight into the number of men either for the military police or for the brigade, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, approximately, and again I understand that you don't know the specific numbers, but approximately how many men would be in a Military Police Platoon?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Between 27 and 31 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And this Military Police Platoon from the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade that was in Zenica, where were they located?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The platoon was located or, rather, the command of the platoon was located in the musical school in Zenica, that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, how many -- approximately how many military policemen of the 303rd Brigade were in Zenica in 1993, and where were they located?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The same. One platoon strong, and they were at the machine engineering faculty. The institute and faculty itself. That's where they were. And a part of them were in town near the Jugoplastika company's facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the 314th brigade, how many military policemen in Zenica and where were they located?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The same thing. The 314th also had one platoon and they were in the upper portion of the institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, the 301st Brigade, same questions.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The 301st Brigade used facility or premises of -- actually, it was in the middle of town. It was the planning centre or planning institute, that building. I can't quite remember what its name was. And in the economical commercial centre part of it. That's where the platoon was. I can't recall the name of it, actually the name of the facility, the premises themselves. But it's a building in the centre of town near the municipality building and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell us again the reason why the 3rd Corps Commander issued the document that you have before you? What was the -- what was the purpose behind him sending this document to these units or to the units to which it's addressed? Why was that done?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Because of what it says here in the preamble. In the introduction it says because of the abuse of the positions by individual members of the military police. For that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any additional information or can you elaborate upon what abuse was being referred to? Did you have any knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: There were situations in which the patrol service was moving around the town itself. There would be five patrols, the military police patrol, the 314th and the 7th Muslim Brigade, and the 303rd. You would have all these patrols patrolling the town, and then you would gain the impression that it was only the police who were there, full the police. And then military personnel were carrying long-barrelled weapons. So I think there was another order that the defence and prosecution could see and that was prohibiting the use of carrying long-barrelled weapons around town without having the insignia of the unit you belonged to displayed on your sleeve. So if a patrol would enter somebody else's premises or apartment or whatever, they would know that this was done by the 3rd Corps police and you wouldn't -- you would know exactly that they were our policemen who were engaged in that and not members of the 314th or 303rd or 7th Muslim or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, this reference to abuses, do you know if it made or in any way was referring to the situation in the music school where the command of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade Military Police Platoon was located?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I really do apologise. I won't come up to expectations but I don't know what the commander had in mind. Perhaps it was because the 7th and 303rd and the military police battalion. I really don't know. I can't say what prompted him to write this order. Now, as for abuse of the military police of the 7th they were equal or similar in behaviour to the behaviour of the other military police forces in my opinion which -- that's my own personal opinion. It need not be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, at any point in 1993, as part of your duties within the 3rd Corps military police battalion, did you ever become aware of persons being abused in the Zenica Music School?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I personally never had any information like that nor was I aware of it, but I know that there was some rumours going round about some kind of abuse, but to my knowledge and awareness from the corps command I think that some humanitarians, perhaps the Red Cross, went to check and investigate. I never received a report of that kind or -- nor do I know that anybody was detained there beyond a certain deadline or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, as a -- as a deputy commander of the military police battalion within the 3rd Corps and as someone with legal training, when you heard these rumours what steps did you take as a military police official to determine if those rumours had any validity to them?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Well, I have to correct you. During that period of time I wasn't the deputy commander of the military police. I was -- yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The witness has just answered and said that at that point in time he wasn't the deputy commander of the military police, and he clearly stated that he had no personal knowledge of any kind of goings-on in the music school. So therefore that is our objection to the manner in which the question was raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In the summer of 1993, sir, what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I was the official to combat crime in Zenica, and I was official officer, and I was engaged in a team set up by the public security station, a member of the team, and set up by the military police and the police department, to uncover crimes, the looting of apartments and burglaries and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So during the summer of 1993, sir, you were responsible or you were involved in combatting crime in Zenica, and a few moments ago, page 52, line 24, you said that you were aware of rumours going around about some kind of abuse, and my question is: As someone who was involved in combatting crime in Zenica, what steps did you take based on these rumours you heard?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: As an individual working to prevent crime, we dealt exclusively with property, crimes against property. That's what I want to point out. And had I had any knowledge about anything else, I would be duty-bound and would have done that. I would have written a report informing my commander or the superior professional organ that something untoward was going on indicating some sort of crime. And to this day I don't know that something was going on which is contrary to the rules and provisions we were working under at the time, in violation of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I take it then, sir, that you disregarded those rumours that you heard about abuse at the music school.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, very often, for example I now work as the official on the part of the army of the federation. I would hear rumours that some young people were -- Mladic was located at Pale, but those are rumours, and there was no trace of that. So if you have propaganda working strongly, and let me quote another case, for example, a very serious rumour, but anybody with any reason couldn't believe that something like that could be put out on the air. For example, in front -- when a shell fell in front of a department store and 16 people were killed, the rumours were that members of the army had taken the people out of the store and killed them. Now, would you have believed that if you had seen what had happened and then hear rumours, different kinds of rumours going round describing the situation differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I take it then, sir, from your answer that in fact when you heard these rumours about abuse in the music school you didn't take any steps at all to determine whether the rumours were true.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn now, sir, to some of the other issues that the Defence have asked you about, and let's start with Dusina. I'd like to ask you, sir -- you told us that you were tasked with going to Lasva with some other military police and transporting surrendered HVO soldiers to the KP Dom. Is that corrected?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, approximately the date and time that you were given this tasking?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I know it was in the evening after 8.00 certainly, after 8.00 p.m. I can't remember exactly. It was the end of January, but I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, if it was the actual day that the combat had occurred in the area around Dusina?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I think it was that day when the fighting stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell us approximately what time it was that you arrived at the school in Lasva?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I apologise. I said I wasn't at the school. I was by the bus and the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where was the bus?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: By the railway station, on the bridge there. I don't know if you know the area, but there's a railway station, a bridge you cross to get to the village over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, can you tell us how far it was from the bridge at the railway station to the school?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: If you were to take the road, the asphalt road, more than 400 metres. If you were to go on foot and take a shortcut used by the locals, then about 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what time -- I assume you went on the bus. You personally travelled from Zenica to the Lasva train station on the bus?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What time did you arrive at the train station in Lasva?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I really wouldn't like to hazard a guess. I don't remember whether it was -- from Zenica to Lasva doesn't take you more than 20 minutes. About 20 minutes roughly. I can't give you an exact time or the exact date. It was in the evening hours at any rate, during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time the bus left the railway station at Lasva?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Forty minutes at the most after our arrival. A group of people had gone to take up -- to take those people, bring them to the bus, and then we went back to Zenica by bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall approximately what time you arrived, then, at the KP Dom on this day?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I don't know what time it was because, believe me, the time wasn't so important to me in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know if it was before or after midnight?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: It was before midnight. I'm sure of that. So if we left about 8.00, by 10.00, half past 10.00 on the outside, we would have returned to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, approximately how many surrendered HVO soldiers did you transport in this bus?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Up to 15 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, sir, were those men, were their identities recorded in any way as they were put onto the bus?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I was a soldier, a policeman, a military policeman tasked to ensure the safe transport of those persons. What the authorised people were doing, the company commanders, the people who took over the prisoners from the school, I really don't know. I know that once we entered the KP Dom, we entered through the main gate, we disembarked from the bus and took them to the receptionist, and that was the end of our task. I was merely a military policeman at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, whether any of the persons, these surrendered HVO soldiers, approximately 15 of whom got on the bus, do you recall if any of them had any visible signs of injury, any wounds, any bleeding, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes. One person, our military officials of the military police, transported one person in a passenger car because he had some injuries. I don't know whether they were inflicted during combat or in some other way, but he was injured, and he was transported by a passenger car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any point in time on that day, sir, did you become aware of the identity of any of these surrendered HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us, sir, that there were, as you put it, the authorised people, the company commanders, the people who took over the prisoners from the school, do you recall the names of any of those persons?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes. One of the authorised persons was Mr. Semir Saric. I didn't know him by name at the time, but I remember a rather strange thing. That man was making a lot of noise. He warned of the Geneva Conventions, take care, don't hurt anyone, and that is how I remember him. And we are good friends to this day when I started working in police investigations. So I remember him in particular. And I remember Nermin Dzambegovic, my company commander, who was an active-duty officer in the JNA and I think he's now working in Gorazde, somewhere in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And both of these two individuals, Mr. Semir Saric and Mr. Nermin Dzambegovic - I'm sorry for the pronunciation - both of those two men were members of your military police unit or the unit you were in, not the --

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than -- other than the military police officers from the 3rd Corps who were present, did you know or recognise or learn the identity of any other 3rd Corps soldiers who were present at the time you were in Lasva?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: We came after the combat operations ended. Around the railway station in Lasva, there were a lot of soldiers close to the tracks. I think they belonged to the Municipal Staff, members of the 7th Muslim Brigade. In fact, I know they were because of someone I knew personally. I heard that he was killed in Zenica. He was a company commander. So I know there were two or three units there and the men of those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us the name of the person that you knew who was later killed in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, the company commander. We had heard in Zenica that he had been killed in combat operations there before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So you were in Zenica when you heard that Mr. Camdzic had been killed but he had been killed in fact in the area around Dusina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, the identity of any of the other 3rd Corps soldiers that you saw present in Lasva on the evening you were there? Again, excluding your fellow military police officers.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: No. I can't now recall the names of those men. The situation was rather tense. We policemen had arrived. No one likes the police. So I wasn't really interested in seeing who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you told us earlier that you were aware that there were dead on both sides due to the conflict in Dusina. When did you first become aware of that, that there had been casualties on both sides during the conflicts in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I'm afraid I haven't understood you properly. When did I first learn about casualties. When we set off to carry out our tasks, we heard that there had been casualties on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's precisely what I was answering -- asking. So by the time you arrived in Lasva at the train station, you were already aware that there had been combat casualties on both sides during the fighting in the area around Dusina?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, and this is I believe my last question about events in Dusina, can you tell us a little bit about the 15 surrendered HVO soldiers that got on the bus? Can you tell us a little bit about, based on perhaps their body language or the way they were moving or the way they were acting, can you tell us a little bit about how their mood was or how their spirits were as they got on that bus?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know whether you were ever in the position of a captive or a prisoner of war or for your life to be at risk during combat. I hope you never have, but somebody participating in combat operations and captured by the opposing side can hardly be expected to feel at ease. I think they were happy to learn that we were going to the KP Dom. The most important thing is to get them away from the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely my point, sir, because the fact that none of those persons felt comfortable speaking to you or any of your fellow military policemen was a direct result of the fact that they didn't feel at ease. They had been captured by forces from your army. One wouldn't expect them to be in a mood to engage you in a conversation.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Exactly. I am not too relaxed even now. If we leave the courtroom, we can joke around, but I don't feel too comfortable even now, and especially when we talk of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand, sir, exactly how you feel. Let me move on now to the incident concerning the kidnapping of Mr. Zivko Totic. You told us, sir, about the steps that you -- that your military police unit was ordered to undertake, and my question, sir, relates more to you personally, that is, what actions, if any, were you personally involved in in terms of trying to discover what had happened to Mr. Zivko Totic?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Personally, we were following a commission led by Mr. Ibrakovic, so I was escorting that commission if we're talking about that particular task. As for other talk with colleagues inquiring into the possibility of who might have done the kidnapping, but we, all of us, endeavoured to find some sort of clue or traces linked to the kidnapping of Mr. Totic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say you were escorting the commission, sir, where did you go? Where did you escort that commission to?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: We went to a village called Arnauti or Gliznik [phoen] or both of those villages. These are two or three villages up near Babina Rijeka. These are localities you're probably not familiar with, or maybe you know more than I do, because I reached Zenica just before the war. So I was providing physical security and trying it assist. I personally didn't enter any of these places. They went into the mosque, into houses. I was in the village looking around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what did you see in the village?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: What did I see in the village? The villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see any foreigners, or people who appeared to be foreigners in the village of Arnauti when you were there that day?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Well, you see, I didn't speak to anyone to be able to say that he was a foreigner. Now, if I let my beard grow and neglect my appearance, I know that -- what you're referring to. There were some bearded men in front of a house, but I couldn't tell if he was a Bosnian or a foreigner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: These people that you saw weren't wearing any type of distinctive clothing that might lead you to believe that they were from the Middle East or of Arab or north African descent?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I didn't look at them carefully regarding their apparel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, you told us that these efforts that were undertaken by military police from the 3rd Corps occurred in the period up to four or five days after Mr. Totic was kidnapped and then that involvement of the 3rd Corps military police ended; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes, correct. That's what I said, four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And during this period that you were in Arnauti, that would be within that four- or five-day window following Mr. Totic's kidnapping?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe towards the end, the 4th or 5th day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall who the members of this commission that you were escorting were? Who were these people in this commission?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I said that one of the members, Mirso Ibrakovic. I think he was commander of the Municipal Staff. I'm not quite sure what his position was. Then there was a representative of the Croatian nation. I don't know the names. Some left already in 1993. I was an ordinary policeman. My task was to ensure the security of these people, to make sure that nobody would disturb them. As soon as they finished their work, my task was over too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall -- do you recall, sir, whose idea it was to go to Arnauti?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: These are political matters. This was -- these were matters dealt with at the corps level and above.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall whether among the members of this commission was anyone from CSB or anyone from any kind of intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, my learned colleague asked you a number of questions about the involvement of military police and the kidnapping, and you told us that there was no involvement by any military police or 3rd Corps security units in this kidnapping. Did you ever become aware, sir, of anyone who was involved in the kidnapping of Zivko Totic?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: According to rumours after the exchange, apparently foreigners who were in Zenica were behind it. I don't know their names and whether that was true or not, but that was the rumour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever hear or whether it was part of your military police duties or otherwise, did you ever hear that an individual named Ramo Durmis was involved in any way in the kidnapping of Zivko Totic?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I did have occasion to hear that name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have heard in this Tribunal the testimony of Mr. Totic, and if we look carefully at the transcript, we will see that he gives answers who could have done that. So I think this question can confuse the witness, and I think it is beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief by my colleague, Mrs. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your response, Mr. Mundis, to the objection of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me try to do this in the presence of the witness to save time. Our position is that my learned colleague from the Defence asked the witness a number of questions about who was responsible for this kidnapping, particularly in an effort to preclude 3rd Corps military police and security units from any involvement in that kidnapping. I would respectfully disagree with my colleague from the Kubura Defence. I believe that the testimony of the previous witness that he's referred to quite clearly indicated that there were certain individuals among those kidnappers who tried to reveal their identity, who pretended to speak a foreign language when in fact they didn't, and who also wearing gloves and taking other steps to disguise perhaps the colour of their skin. And I believe that the witness would have some information that would shed some light on this issue for the Chamber but it's clearly not beyond the scope of the direct examination in the first place, and in the second place we would respectfully disagree with the evidence as described and as it relates to a previous witness who has testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the Defence had to do with Ramo Durmis. You referred to Totic's testimony, who according to you mentioned Mr. Durmis. Can you give us a reference, a precise reference, or is this a leading question that you're putting to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I didn't say that Mr. Totic mentioned Ramo Durmis by name. What I did say is Mr. Totic talked about individuals who pretended to speak Arabic but didn't, and he spoke about individuals who wore gloves to the colour of their skin or shade of their skin couldn't be visible. That leads directly to an inference that local people were involved with or in conjunction with the Arabs or the foreigners. I believe that I have a good faith basis for asking this series of questions on cross-examination. It clearly arises out of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. direct examination by the Hadzihasanovic team. We have a good faith basis for doing this in cross-examination, Mr. President, as you note we are certainly entitled to ask leading questions when we have a good faith basis for doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to the Defence, I will summarise the position of the Prosecution. The Prosecution tells us on page 64, line 23 and onwards, that when Mr. Totic testified, he indicated that those who captured him and who pretended to be Arabs could in fact have been locals who masked themselves and that within that framework he wanted to ask a question about Mr. Durmis. That is the position of the Prosecution. I saw the Defence attorney on her feet. What does she wish to tell us since on line 3209 the following is stated by Totic: "The kidnapper spoke in Arabic except for the locals who pretended to speak Arabic but they couldn't speak it correctly." This is line 319. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on the basis of what you have just read and my own examination, I think that the question put to the witness mentioning a certain name is not appropriate nor does it have any grounds in the previous testimony nor in my examination-in-chief. I think the Prosecution has to find out first from the witness whether he knows that, in addition to foreigners, any other persons were involved. Does he know that there were people pretending to speak foreign languages. And I don't know how he could come to the name of a particular person. To put into the witness's mouth a name that was not mentioned at all I think is inappropriate for the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mundis. The Defence is indicating that you mentioned directly the name of Durmis, and the Defence is asking how did you reach that name since there were no preliminary stages in your questioning leading to go Durmis. Apparently the other Defence team have something to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. A point of clarification. I think that the witness has already answered that he heard that the Mujahedin were behind this. Now, our learned colleague should explain the link between the persons mentioned by Mr. Totic, that is possibly people who were Bosniaks and who didn't speak Arabic well, and Ramiz Durmis -- Ramo Durmis who did the colleague mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As the Prosecution has repeatedly committed when the Defence objects, what we are required to do is have a good faith basis to put our questions to the witness during cross-examination. There is not a need for a lengthy foundation to be laid. There is simply a need for us to have a good faith basis. We believe we have that good faith basis. We -- I have -- I have explained to the Trial Chamber precisely where we're trying to go, and once again this series of objections has consumed significantly more time than would have been the case had the witness been allowed to continue the answer that he gave us. He did say, as my learned colleague from the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead with your question, because we are wasting time, and the Judges will judge the relevance of the questions. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you just told us or prior to this discussion you told us that you had heard of the name Ramo Durmis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you hear that name in connection with the events concerning the kidnapping of Mr. Totic?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear, but let me add something. Whenever something was wrong in Zenica involving foreigners was linked to Ramo Durmis. So this could have been true or not true. So that person was not important for me, nor did I have any contact with him to be able to say more about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell me why that person, Ramo Durmis, was not important to you, sir? How did you reach that conclusion that he was not important to you?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The first time I heard of that man and his name there was a combat operations in the surroundings of Visoko, and allegedly from that moment on the man left the army. No one knew his real status, who he was or where he came from and who he belonged to, and from that moment on, he was not a member of the army. And as the army and the military police had no knowledge that he acted against military property, military facilities and other acts that are prosecuted by the District Military Court, we as the police were not interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But, sir, can you tell us what you mean by the man left the army? Was he discharged or demobilised?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: If he may have had access to army. Now, whether he was a legal member of the army, I really don't know, but I do know he took part in combat operations in Visoko, and because of some failures and the killing of people he was fighting with, from that moment on he was not accessible to us or to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn now, sir, to a different topic, and that is the steps that the 3rd Corps military police battalion took with respect to the monastery at Guca Gora. Do you recall, sir, the date that you and your fellow military policemen were first ordered to go to Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I think it was -- I'm afraid I have a problem with dates, but I think it was the 15th or the 16th of June. 15th and the 16th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, how many military policemen went with you from the 3rd Corps military police battalion in mid-June when you went to Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: We used a minibus for transport, a small bus that can accommodate 16. So there was me, another authorised official person, and the rest were policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you give me a rough number? Was the minibus full? You said it could accommodate 16, but was the minibus full?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you arrived at the monastery in Guca Gora in mid-June 1993, how many other ABiH 3rd Corps soldiers or military policemen were present at the monastery at the time you arrived?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: You're asking me how many members of the military police of the 306th joined us. One squad, about ten men. If we're talking about members of the BH army, ten men. So there was a total of about 26 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the squad of military police from the 306th Mountain Brigade, they were already present when you arrived in Guca Gora, or did they arrive at about the same time as you, or did they arrive after you?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: We found them there by the command post. A military police squad were there. They joined us. I don't know where they came from. I don't know where they were before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you told us, sir, that it was difficult to enter the facility, and then you a few moments after that spoke about the presence of Arabs. Was it difficult to enter the facility because of the presence of the Arabs or was there another reason why it was difficult to enter the facility?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was some of us who speak the language. The people inside were the only impediment. Otherwise, we could have entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it then, sir, from your answer that there were some of the military policemen from the 3rd Corps military police battalion or the 306th Mountain Brigade military police squad who spoke Arabic?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: No. That's not what I said. What I said was this: With the Arabs inside the premises, there were our men there, locals, Bosnians, and all communication went through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, because the English transcript certainly leads one to a different conclusion. Now, sir, when you got there, I take it because you -- you've kept referring to people being inside, all of these Arabs were inside the monastery when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: This group, the group I'm talking about, was inside. We saw some of them, and others appeared later on when they were supposed to come out. So they were within the gates. I don't know whether you know what Guca Gora looks like, but they were inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this then, sir: Were they inside the church building part of the monastery or inside the gated courtyard that is immediately adjacent to the church building?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Some people that we hadn't seen were inside the church, whereas others were within the gated courtyard, the stone slabs that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many of these foreign people would you estimate were present in total on the grounds or in the buildings of the Guca Gora monastery?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I think the total number -- once again I don't want to hazard a guess nor did I count them, but there were not more than 25. Twenty to 25, I would say. But you could get into the monastery from another entrance. I don't know if you know the area. I was there for two or three days. I went to investigate. There could have been 20, 25 at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how many local Bosnians were with those Arab individuals?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Altogether, both, 20 to 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So there was a total of 20 to 25 Arabs and locals that were present and approximately 25 military policemen from the 3rd Corps military police battalion and the 306th military police squad. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What kind of armaments if any did the Arabs and locals who were in the monastery have?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: At the very entrance, whether it was a machine-gun or some heavy weaponry of another kind, all the rest was infantry weapons, ordinary infantry weapons, and on our side the same. We did have a sniper here or there. We were a bit better equipped than what they had, but that would be roughly it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I don't believe this is clear from the transcript, sir, but of the 20 to 25 Arabs and locals who were present, how many of them were Arabs and how many of them were local Bosnians?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I talked to one of them, shouted at one of them. I don't know how many there were, some of ours, some of them, but I talked to one particular man. And if I were to see him today without his beard, I would find it difficult to recognise him. But I talked to one of them. There were more inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So I take it then, sir, that it's not really possible to -- for you to give us a rough estimate of the breakdown between the Arabs and the locals who were present in the monastery; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: You're right, yes. Your assumptions are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, what eventually happened to this group of 20 to 25 locals and Arabs who were in the monastery? Where did they go? What did they do? How did you get them to leave? Can you tell us a little bit more about that?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Well, we didn't get them to leave. In a way, we threatened that we would bring in reinforcements, that we would shoot, and they threatened to shoot at us too. And finally, if I can use a civilian expression, we reached an agreement, and then we entered the premises. And that was our goal. It wasn't our intention to arrest anybody. All we wanted to do was to get into the premises and to protect it and to prevent an escalation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why was it not your intention to arrest anyone who was present?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Well, since I was the senior there by way of rank and age, my assessment was that we didn't have -- that we couldn't arrest them, that there was nobody we could single out and arrest. So that was the basic reason. And we wouldn't have achieved the assignment we were sent there to achieve and from Zenica to Guca Gora is quite a long way away. So we couldn't expect reinforcements to come in and help us out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What -- can you elaborate or explain to us what you mean when you say, "There was nobody we could single out and arrest?" What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: If we were literally to apply the rules and regulations, we ought to have arrested all of them, because we saw devastations on the building, which means that private property was being devastated. So we would have had to have arrested them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I take it also in light of the orders that you'd received that you told us about earlier to protect religious facilities. That would be another reason to take special precautions in terms of arresting these people?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: It was our aim to enter the facility and protect it from being destroyed any further. That's what I said a moment ago. That was our main goal. We wanted to fulfil the assignment we had been given in Zenica to protect the facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But you didn't arrest anyone who was present on the grounds or in the buildings of the monastery on that day?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: No. No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where did these people go?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: They went towards Travnik, towards the village. We didn't follow them. We didn't have the need to follow them. All we wanted to do was to get inside the premises and to place guards on both sides, on both -- at both the entrances, and we did what we were sent to do. We accomplished the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I take it, sir, that these people had some kind of vehicles and they just exited the monastery grounds and got in their vehicles and drove off towards Travnik?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I didn't see any vehicles. I think there was one just underneath the monastery, below the monastery, but I didn't go to see. I saw one myself, and that was on the curve, the first curve you could see. I didn't see any others. Some went on foot. Others went -- well, I don't know how they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the direction that they were going was area that was controlled by units of the 3rd Corps. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I doubt that they would have gone to the area under the HVO control, although it wasn't that far off. So, yes, I would say they went offer to the area controlled by the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, was this the first time that you were aware of the presence of any of these foreigners or, more specifically, Arabs in the 3rd Corps area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: When I learnt of their existence. Well, I saw them. I would see them. I would see Arabs in Zenica and on the roads towards Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see armed foreigners in Zenica in 1993?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I didn't see them with rifles, but I can't guarantee that they didn't have them. Towards the end of 1993, yes. Yes, I did see them armed as well. There were those who were armed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was this incident at Guca Gora -- or not incident but this series of events that you've described for us in mid-June 1993 in Guca Gora, was this the first time that you'd ever encountered any of these armed foreigners during the course of your military police duties?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I personally -- well, I'm talking about myself. I had no contact with them, which means I didn't have any conflicts with them or anything else. Once again, let me say there was an incident. I was called to the police administration because allegedly they had taken into custody some members of the army who were Arabs. I arrived there, and when we asked to see the identity papers of the person who had been taken into custody, he didn't have any, and he showed us a UNHCR card. And as of that moment on, that person wasn't of any interest to us. And when I went back to my unit, I said it wasn't a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So you were aware, sir, if I understand what you've said, there was an incident where one of these foreigners attempted to take people out of the army, take -- it says here take members of the army out of -- let me try again. "They had taken into custody some members of the army who were Arabs." Can you explain that to us, please?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I do apologise. I don't seem to be speaking clearly enough. What I said was this: We were informed by the duty policeman from the police station in Zenica that in their premises they had one member of the military who was a foreigner, and he introduced himself as being a member of the BH army. That's how he represented himself. I and a colleague of mine went to the police department to be present while he was being questioned because he was allegedly found in a stolen car. So it was one man. And when we arrived there, we asked to see his identification papers. And when we established that he wasn't a member of the army of the BH, that he had no proof of being an army member, we went back and that's where our responsibilities ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see the time, too, and I was getting a bit worried there. How much longer do you need, Mr. Mundis, to complete your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would -- I will review that during the course of the break. My understanding is that the Defence for Hadzihasanovic took about an hour and 28 minutes by my calculation. I can discuss this with the registrar. Do I have a number other issues I'd like to address with the witness. I would be prepared, if the -- I understand the time constraints. I would be prepared to try to pair that down. It would be helpful if the Chamber had questions, if you could give me a rough idea and I could take that into consideration as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have the additional questions that have to be asked. So we understood yesterday that this witness needed to leave today because he had other business to attend to and couldn't stay until Monday, over the weekend. Now, how many -- how much time do you need for your questions, Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would say, as things now stand, ten more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if it's ten minutes, this leaves 45 minutes afterwards. I had some questions myself, but we can sacrifice those questions because we were told that the witness has to leave today. I know that there was another witness that was waiting, so, Mr. Registrar, could you tell the other witness that he will be coming back on Monday afternoon. He doesn't have to wait. We'll be starting with him at quarter past two Monday afternoon. And we have to end these proceedings today at 1.45, so we're going to have 45 minutes left to get through everything. We will be back here at five to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me just ask you one or two more questions about the time you were in Guca Gora or actually more specifically after Guca Gora. What kind of report, whether oral or written, did you give your superiors concerning what you had observed in Guca Gora in mid-June 1993?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I orally reported to my immediate superior about the events in Guca Gora and then regular reports began coming in, written ones, from Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So you informed your commander, Mr. Mujezinovic, about what you had seen on the presence of these Arabs in the monastery in mid-June 1993?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a few questions, sir, about your relationship in general to Mr. Mujezinovic, the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion commander. In a typical, say, workday, how much interaction did you have with him in 1993?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: During 1993, very little. Perhaps once a day or not even once a day. Sometimes once a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During 1993, sir, did you spend most of your -- well, let me ask you this: Where was the military police, the 3rd Corps military police battalion headquartered?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: In the Zenica KP Dom. They -- that's where they were. This was given over to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, did you maintain an office there or was there a dedicated space that was allocated to the battalion?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: They used five facilities, but where we worked myself and the rest of the members of the military police platoon were on the ground floor in the command building. So the last building. That was the battalion command. And the premises used by military police investigations, and I had my office there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did Mr. Mujezinovic also have an office in the same building or in one of these other buildings?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: In that same building but the other entrance, an entrance on the other side and on the upper storey. The first floor, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I take, sir, from your answers that you gave earlier this morning, Mr. Mujezinovic reported to Mr. Dugalic?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who in turn reported directly to the 3rd Corps commander. That answer, sir, wasn't reflected in the transcript. Could you please say it maybe a little louder.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic reported to Mr. Dugalic, who reported to the 3rd Corps commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, during 1993, did you personally have any involvement in directly briefing the 3rd Corps commander on any issues relating to military police work?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell me a little bit about the units within the military police battalion of the 3rd Corps in the sense of -- you've told us there were four companies and a couple of smaller units including an investigation unit and a counter-terrorism or anti-terrorism unit. Who gave the taskings to the companies and these other two smaller units within the battalion?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The battalion commander of the military police. He issued tasks to the commanders of units or companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you've told us, sir, about how each of the companies had a specific task or function; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, who the commanders of these four companies were during 1993?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall. The first company was Dzambegovic, Nermin Dzambegovic. After him, there was -- what was his name? Faik, Faik something. I can't remember the surname. Faik Skopljak, I think, the commander of the 1st company after Dzambegovic. The commander of the 2nd Company was Zead Ganic, and then Fetic Suad was the 3rd Company commander. The PTD [Realtime transcript read in error "PTT"] unit at that stage was Mirza, Mirza something. I can't remember the surname. He left fairly soon. And then there was Hasim, and finally there was the leader or commander of the traffic group, Cago Ibrahim. And afterwards it was Mustafic, Mevludin Mustafic, and finally the military police investigations, Bakir Alispahic, and then after him, Ruzmir Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, in the English transcript there is abbreviation. It says the PTT unit. This is on page 79, line 25. Can you tell us, first of all, if that's a correct abbreviation, and second of all, what that stands for.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The abbreviation is not PTT but PTD. PTD is the acronym, unit for anti-terrorist activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you told us in general terms earlier this morning what the PTD unit did. I'm wondering if you can elaborate for us a little bit in terms of what type of anti-terrorist activities this unit was conducting and perhaps explain to us, if you know, the nature of the terrorist threat that the 3rd Corps was seeking to alleviate.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: This battalion of the military police was established to resemble the JNA battalions with slight amendments, and within those units there were also the PTD units as we will called them, and the establishment of that union, I don't know how it came about but I know the union had a separate task to discipline the army of the federation because it was made up of, let's say, military policemen mostly. They were trained better later on, but that was in the final stages of the war and the conflict with the HVO. But towards the end of the war, they were better trained and had better equipment. So these were young guys who -- well, they were sportsmen and were able to provide security for various personages, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I asked this, sir, and you've explained it was a structure that mirrored that of the JNA, but it just struck me as a bit odd that an anti-terrorist unit would have a role in discipline and I'm just wondering why that was the case, if you can perhaps explain or shed a little light on that.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that all the units had their own permanent assignments, and they implemented them to the letter. This unit, and I can freely say that, was a little freer by way of deployment, that is to say it didn't have fixed security assignments. We could use it as an intervention unit if we needed to send out a patrol, for example. We could send a patrol into town for the curfew, to ensure curfew. So that's what I mean by discipline. And they were readily recognisable. They had -- wielded certain respect in Zenica. People knew about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just so we're clear then, sir, this anti-terrorist or counter-terrorist unit, did it have any specific responsibilities with respect to the Arabs that you've talked about or the armed foreigners, the armed Arabs that were in the 3rd Corps area?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: In that stage it dealt with itself more than it dealt with others during that initial stage of formation. So during that initial phase it had no assignments. Later on it was used when there were some more serious takings into custody and so on to form a unit which would be the fulcrum of the battalion, but that was later on, 1994 and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what -- what unit were you referring to when you said the fulcrum of the battalion in 1994? What is that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: It took part in arresting the Green Legion, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a little bit more about the battalion, the 3rd Corps military police battalion's structure. How many staff officers were part of the command of the battalion? Was the battalion structured like other battalions, like an infantry battalion in terms of a staff for the battalion command itself?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: The battalion command of the military police was a little specific compared to the other infantry battalions, for example. So in the command of the battalion, we had an assistant for educational affairs, for personnel affairs, logistics, because there was no security officer within the battalion, for example, like the Mountain Battalions did. But we did have a man dealing with things like that in addition to all the other assignments. And I think this came under the security organ. They had an assistant for financial matters, and that's what it had. In the battalions you could have an assistant commander, mountain battalions assistant commander for communications, for example, because it didn't have a communications man, a signalsman. So this was an operative and an educational and training organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the battalion -- the military police battalion of the 3rd Corps have a duty system or a duty roster so there was always duty officers 24 hours a day, seven days a week?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Within the battalion itself, there was duty in companies. There was the duty officer of the battalion. In addition to that, in military police investigations there was a department for 24-hour duty service, and this was on duty round the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I assume that there were some kind of regular battalion meetings whether on a daily or other regular schedule?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: If you're talking about 1993, I can't tell you with certainty because I wasn't a member of the battalion command. I was later on, and I know how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you -- I neglected to ask you one question earlier when we were talking about the events in Lasva and Dusina. You told us that when the HVO -- surrendered HVO soldiers arrived at KP Dom there was some kind of a receptionist at the KP Dom. Can you tell us, was that receptionist part of the army or was that a civilian person, and what exactly was the role of this receptionist at the KP Dom who -- to whom these surrendered HVO soldiers were transferred?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we took this unit to the centre for prisoners of war. From the moment they were taken into custody, the people who were securing this military prison and the centre for prisoners of war took care of them and only official persons in charge of the investigation could have contact with them. The military police finishes its task upon delivering them to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Sir, let me ask you just a couple of questions about the military offence or military crime of desertion. What steps, if any, did military police officers of the 3rd Corps military police battalion take with respect to deserters?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I have to admit it may not be a good thing, but desertion was quite widespread. Soldiers were leaving units, going to another unit without telling anyone, and the military police in that situation would start a search for such persons. That would be the first phase, to try and contact them physically. If it was not possible to find them, then I don't know. Other methods were applied such as checking the records, issuing a wanted poster for such persons, and if we don't find them, there's nothing much we can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But it certainly wasn't the case that by deserting a soldier could somehow unilaterally sever his or her ties with the military?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I don't know what leads you to such a conclusion. He may sever it. He may escape beyond the borders, beyond the control -- area controlled by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me -- let me ask you this same question in a slightly different way. An individual, a person who is in the army, remains in the army from a legal point of view until they're demobilised or discharged; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: A person who is in the army, if we're talking about mobilisation. If we're talking about a mobilised person abandoning the army or somebody who is doing his military service, once he leaves the army he is for another 30 days a member of the army. After that, he is eliminated for -- from the roster, from the register.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So a person, in 1993, who left the army without permission or without being demobilised, would that person remain subject to arrest by the military police and trial by a District Military Court, again in 1993 during the war, or could a soldier just simply quit the army and the army had no recourse with respect to that person?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: If a military officer leaves the unit and a unit starts a search for such a person, and this is entrusted to the military police, then the military police should arrest him, and then he's sanctioned according to the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We had a few other issues, but I think in light of the time as well as giving everyone an opportunity who has any remaining questions, we'll stop our cross-examination at this point. I do thank you, Colonel, for answering our questions today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mahir, you said that when you set off to arrest captured members of the HVO and transport them from Lasva that you already knew that commander Camdzic had been killed. How did you known commander Camdzic?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I knew him from sight. We weren't friends, but I did know him. I don't know how we learnt. Somebody probably reported that he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to a question from my learned friend, you also said that before you left, you knew that in Dusina soldiers had been killed on both sides. Tell me, please, in wartime is it customary when there are combat operations somewhere for there to be casualties on both sides or was this a shocking piece of news for you?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Madam Residovic, as I know that you were in Sarajevo and you know how many people were killed, I think that even families couldn't mourn their dead. So that the death of a colleague of ours became almost normal. We knew the man had been killed, and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But more precisely, is it normal when you heard that there were combat operations, is it also normal to hear that there were casualties on both sides, on the enemy side and among your own ranks, or is this something exceptional?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: It is only normal for people to be killed on both sides and to have casualties on both sides. There was a war on, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahir, when you set off with your assignment to Guca Gora, at that point in time were you already aware that the monastery was at risk from some persons?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes. We knew that the monastery needed to be protected from destruction. That is what we were told. We have to prevent it from being destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the reason that you had better weapons, as you told us, because you expected to come across people who were holding to the facility by force?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We took a unit that could deal with the problem confronting it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was your main task when you set off? Did the task relate to the monastery itself or something else? Was it the monastery and the church that you were tasked to protect?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Our task was to enter the monastery and prevent it from being destroyed, and that facility was called the monastery in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you got there you said that you saw a group of some 20 armed Arabs and some locals with them, and you described your efforts to remove them from the facility. Tell me, please, for you as the leader of that group, was it most important for you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we simply object to the first two lines of that question. I repeatedly asked the witness if he could tell us how many Arabs and how many locals there were, and he was unable to do so. I think the testimony was 20 to 25 people in total including both the Arabs and the locals. And perhaps it's just the interpretation, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Maybe I was mistaken in not saying 25, but my understanding was that was the total number of locals and foreigners. I think I was misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Mahir, was: When you got there, did you realise that the monastery was in real danger from these men?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Madam, we were told on leaving that it had to be protected, that they were threatening to destroy it and blow it up. When they wouldn't let us enter, what conclusion could we reach? If they let them stay there, the only conclusion we could make would be that they would destroy it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, in your lengthy endeavours to have them leave the facility, you gave them ultimatums and you were ready to open fire.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I said. There were threats on both sides. We threatened to bring in reinforcements from Zenica, that another unit would come to assist us although we didn't have any such unit, but we tried in every possible way without any losses to enter the monastery.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Had you resorted to force immediately or arrested one of those 25 persons, would that have, according to your conviction at the time, jeopardised the safety of the monastery and lead to consequences that you were meant to prevent?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I made the decision, and I claim that it was right. And now in the same circumstances, I would make the same decision. I wouldn't try to arrest anyone. I would protect the facility I was sent to protect. And then there are other people who will arrest, establish the identity, and do all those other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to a question from -- no. Let me ask you something else first. Tell me, please, as you were first a policeman and then engaged in investigations, were those foreigners members of the army?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I told you of one case when I was able to see for myself that they were not at that moment. Now, whether each and every foreigner belonged somewhere, I don't know, but for us they were not members of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the question of my learned colleague about the music school and your knowledge about it, you said that you had heard some rumours and that you yourself didn't go there. Do you know, Mr. Mahir, whether other members of the battalion had the task to check out those -- those reports or members of the 3rd Corps security? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Madam, I can only tell you what I know. As far as I know, members of the military security sector did enter and control the facility. I really don't know because I wasn't there. I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what they found out as a result of the control?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Had they found out anything, they would have acted in the same way as we would have. If they had found anything, there would have been no music school.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And finally my learned friend asked you about this situation: If a soldier deserts a unit does he really remain in the unit or not. You mentioned the example of Ramo Durmis, for instance, who during fighting in 1992 deserted and headed for the hills. Tell me, these persons who leave the unit or desert the unit, does the unit have effective command and control over that person?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I told you that he -- once he is scrapped from the records, he becomes a civilian. That person is no longer a military serviceman. When arresting people who still haven't joined the unit, they are escapees and only the Ministry of the Interior can have any jurisdiction over them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question is linked to what you just said but in a different situation. If a military unit commander of any level, battalion, brigade, or corps, doesn't do what the law says, that is remove him from the records and that person has deserted, does that commander have effective control and command over that person?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: You can't have effective control over a person as soon as he has gone. He's no longer under your control or command. You can't give him any orders. Even if he didn't remove him from the list, he's on the list of the unit, but the law prescribes that he should be scrapped from the records, returned to the Ministry of the Interior, and then he is under the jurisdiction of other institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the military police, in 1993 and later, did you come across lists of units including many combatants who were not in the unit at all or who had left the unit without being removed from the record?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, but some people were killed. Their family members were proving that they had been killed, but they were on the list. Transfers from one unit to another, from 181st. That was the Foca brigade which was on Mount Igman. Do you know how many people crossed over to the 1st Corps units? They were in the records of the 1st Corps and the 3rd Corps and there were searches for them. And to what extent the personnel officer kept track of all these changes should be explained by people responsible for personnel, why such omissions were made.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We'll just take up one minute for the sake of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think on page 67 of the transcript, you were saying that Ramo Durmis was not a member of the army since the operation in Visoko. Could you tell us when that operation took place?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: If you're asking me the exact date, I don't know, but I think it was in the first half of December 1992. There was no 3rd Corps at the time. District units and some other local units tried to make a breakthrough towards Sarajevo. In December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I have a few small questions for you. Answering a question from the Defence, you said that there were problems. You conducted investigations, and you mentioned three types of investigations. One regarding the 314th, the Green Legion. You spoke about the Turk guerrilla, and a third investigation that began in the month of May and which ended in September, and the perpetrators were judged in 1994, and you spoke about the mountain guerrilla, and my understanding was that they were called the Falcons or Black Falcons. And you told us that you were ready to provide details about this mountain guerrilla. What can you tell us, to the best of your recollection of course.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: There was a unit that was called mountain guerrilla or Falcons, Sokolovi. These were one in the same unit, members of the 7th Muslim Brigade. A part of them were engaged in criminal acts which were later sanctioned. I mention just two or three typical examples. I was talking about the period of investigations. I can tell you when it took us one hour to find the perpetrator of a criminal offence. Only one hour went by from the moment he acted to his arrest. For instance, opening fire in town or stealing property or fighting amongst themselves. But more complicated cases took several months and sometimes seven or eight months even.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But these young men who were members of this unit called the Sokolovi, what did they do as an offence.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: This group, which included civilians, Hazic Jasmin was a civilian, this is a group for which we had evidence that they had committed at least eight criminal offences, some of which were burglaries, attacks on the parish house in Crkvice, various forms of robbery, of motor vehicles, break-ins into houses, and they stole at least three or four vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question: The military police, could you describe to us the typical apparel of a military policeman? Did he have a uniform? What was the insignia? What were his weapons? What did a military policeman look like?
