As you were such and you even had a command position, could you describe what a military policeman looked like as compared to a soldier of any other unit?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: In the first stage when the army was being formed, including the 3rd Corps, he looked awful. He didn't look like a military policeman. But our aim was to have the unit made recognisable. In addition to the truncheon, a pistol and white belts and white insignia, we endeavoured, not me but the superior command, endeavoured as soon as possible to provide military police insignia for this unit so that they would be recognisable in town and wherever they went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did they have insignia with the words "military police" in your own language written on it?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I said, first badges were made, and afterwards we had insignia on the sleeves because this badge was rather small. But when we had "VP", "military police," on the sleeves, then it was more easily visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question. Concerning the investigations that you undertook, I shall start from an ultra simple case. Let us imagine that in any unit there is a soldier who steals the shoes of another soldier. The soldier victim says that his colleague stole him his boots. What will happen with respect to disciplinary sanction or penal prosecution? Who decides what will be done following the complaint of the soldier?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, those shoes are not worth anything, so the damage is insignificant. If it were an act or an offence which had more significant consequences, like the stealing of his rifle, the commander of that unit through his security organ would be responsible for calling that person to account. So if it's a weapon that is stolen, he would go to the District Military Court. If it's insignificant, then he will be held accountable through disciplinary measures. But it is the commander through his security organs who would issue the steps to be taken in such an event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just have one, perhaps two questions arising from those of Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall the names of any of the mountain guerrilla or the Falcons that you've told us about?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Guerrillas. Well, I can give you all their nicknames. Isakovic Kasim, nicknamed Kale. Hazic Jasmin, nicknamed Kazi [phoen]. Miki's surname I cannot remember, but Fuad was his name. I can't remember his surname. So yes I can. If you want to I can send you their names and surnames. And if you have the criminal list -- register, then you will be able to see and that they were given prison sentences ranging from four to eight years and that they served their sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mahir, with respect to the question asked you by the President of this Trial Chamber, your answer -- you answered who decided on whether somebody will be held accountable through disciplinary measures if he committed an offence, grave or lesser grave. Tell me, the military police of the military unit, did it have rights and duties prescribed for it by law to be taken -- to take steps against perpetrators itself, or did it have to wait in each particular case to be given permission or issued an order to do so?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: This is called filing a report. A military policeman files a report. That's what happens first. If an individual is held back, held in custody, then we file a criminal report to our superior. So the military police could file criminal reports against the perpetrators of misdemeanors, offences or crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And could it do this for crimes?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes. It was duty-bound to do so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mahir, you have already confirmed that the individuals you took into custody and conducted an investigation about were from the Sokolovi or Falcon unit and that they were taken to the military court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: I think they were taken to the higher military court, so they were sentenced by the higher court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm saying that during the investigation, you had complete support and cooperation by the military police of the 7th Muslim brigade and the security service of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Sir, not only did we have it but we were arresting their people. So we were duty-bound to inform them about that. But this didn't stop us and when we went out to prove they were the perpetrators, of course, we did have support, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So that means you had full support from the military security of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IZET MAHIR
utterances.text: Yes, and we asked them for many documents and evidence that those individuals were on the spotted at the given time, which we were trying to prove that they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Colonel. Your testimony has come to an end. I thank all the parties concerned, and thank you for keeping your questions so short enabling us to end today's proceedings on time. I thank you for your contribution, Colonel, and on behalf of the Judges, best wishes for bon voyage back home and for your further military activities. I'm going to ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. I would like to take advantage of this opportunity while the microphone is still on to thank you all and for keeping it brief, the Prosecution and the Defence and Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have just a few more seconds left. Would any -- if the Prosecution has nothing to add. I'm looking towards the Defence. Mr. Dixon is signifying he does not have anything more to add. It is 1.45. We shall reconvene Monday afternoon at quarter past two when we shall be continuing the cross-examination of the witness we started yesterday. Thank you all. Until Monday, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 7th day of February, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
